 If you've been putting off getting your REAL ID and plan to fly this Thanksgiving, you could be facing an unexpected $45 fee at the airport. For the first time during the busy Thanksgiving travel season, passengers without a REAL ID-compliant license or another acceptable form of identification will have to use the Transportation Security Administration's (TSA) paid identity verification process if they still want to fly.

 The TSA began enforcing REAL ID requirements in May 2025 and introduced its $45 TSA ConfirmID fee on February 1, 2026. The process gives travelers without acceptable identification another opportunity to verify their identity. However, the fee has raised concerns about its financial impact on families , particularly those traveling with multiple adults who need to pay. And even after paying, there's no guarantee travelers will make it through security.
 With Thanksgiving already one of the busiest times of year for air travel, understanding the requirements before leaving home could mean the difference between catching your flight and missing it . Here's what travelers need to know.

 What Is The $45 TSA Fee, And Why Does It Exist?
 TSA security check Credit: Shutterstock 
 The TSA introduced its $45 ConfirmID fee on February 1, 2026, giving domestic air travelers without acceptable identification a paid alternative to the standard identity verification process. The fee applies to adults 18 and older who arrive at airport security without a REAL ID-compliant driver's license, passport, or another TSA-approved form of identification.
 According to the TSA's December 2025 announcement, the fee helps cover the additional cost of verifying a passenger's identity rather than passing that expense along to taxpayers. The agency reported that more than 94% of passengers were already presenting acceptable identification at the time of announcement.
 The important distinction is that the $45 payment covers an attempt to verify your identity, not guaranteed access to your flight . TSA officers must still establish that you are who you claim to be before allowing you through security. If they cannot confirm your identity, you may be denied entry to the checkpoint, even after paying.
 How Long Does The $45 Fee Last?
 Travelers at a Transportation Security Administration (TSA) queue at a U.S. airport Credit: David Tran Photo / Shutterstock 
 One benefit of TSA ConfirmID is that the $45 fee covers a 10-day travel period , rather than a single flight. For Thanksgiving travelers taking a short round-trip vacation or visiting family for several days, that means one payment may cover both the departure and return flights, provided they fall within the same 10-day window.
 However, travelers whose return flight falls outside that period would need to pay again if they still lack acceptable identification. The fee is also charged per person, so two adults traveling together without acceptable IDs could face $90 in verification fees.
 How To Pay And Process TSA ConfirmID At The Airport
 Illustrative Editorial of TSA.GOV website homepage. The TSA logo is visible on the display screen. Credit: Shutterstock 
 Travelers who know they will need TSA ConfirmID should complete the payment process before heading to the airport . The TSA recommends paying online in advance to avoid additional delays at security, particularly during busy travel periods.
 ConfirmID Is A Three-Step Process
 Pay the $45 fee online . Visit the official TSA ConfirmID Website and follow the payment instructions through Pay.gov . Payment options include credit cards, debit cards, bank transfers, PayPal, and Venmo.
 Save your payment confirmations . Keep the confirmation email or receipts on your phone, or print a copy to bring with you. You'll need proof of payment when directed to the TSA ConfirmID process.
 Complete identity verification . Follow airport instructions and present your payment confirmation to TSA personnel. Officers will attempt to verify your identity through an alternative screening process before determining whether you can proceed through security.
 Passengers who arrive without paying can generally find payment instructions at designated locations near airport security checkpoints. However, the process may differ depending on the airport, and travelers should not assume they can complete it as quickly as a standard ID check.
 Allow Extra Time During Thanksgiving Week
 TSA officer handling REAL ID to a traveler Credit: Shutterstock 
 Thanksgiving is already one of the busiest times of the year for air travel, and the additional identity verification process could mean even longer waits at security. TSA warns that passengers using ConfirmID should expect delays. Travelers relying on the service should consider allowing an extra 45 to 60 minutes beyond their normal holiday airport arrival time . This is a precautionary recommendation rather than an official TSA estimate, and processing could take longer depending on passenger volume and individual circumstances.
 Free Alternatives To Paying The $45 REAL ID Fee
 US Passport Credit: GOQ / Unsplash 
 The good news is that travelers don't necessarily need a REAL ID driver's license to avoid paying the $45 fee. Although the federal requirements have been in effect since May 7, 2025, the TSA accepts several other forms of identification for domestic flights.
 A valid U.S. passport is one of the easiest alternatives, but it isn't the only option. According to TSA's official identification requirements , travelers can also present the following documents instead of a REAL ID-compliant state license.
 U.S. passport or U.S. passport card : Both are acceptable for domestic air travel.
 Foreign government-issued passport : An acceptable alternative for international visitors and other eligible travelers.
 DHS Trusted Traveler cards : Global Entry, NEXUS, SENTRI, and FAST cards are accepted.
 Military identification : U.S. Department of Defense IDs, including those issued to military dependents.
 Permanent Resident Card : Commonly known as a Green Card.
 Enhanced Driver's License (EDL) : State-issued enhanced licenses and identification cards qualify, even if they don't display the standard REAL ID star.
 Other acceptable documents include certain federally recognized Tribal identification cards, Transportation Worker Identification Credentials (TWIC), and Veteran Health Identification Cards (VHIC). However, some travelers have reported problems getting TSA officers to accept federally recognized Tribal IDs , despite their inclusion on the agency's list of approved identification.
 A temporary paper driver's license is not considered acceptable identification by the TSA. If you're planning to upgrade your license before Thanksgiving, make sure you have received the physical REAL ID card or have another approved document available before traveling.
 Travelers should also know that children under 18 generally do not need identification when traveling domestically with an adult. However, airlines may have their own requirements for minors, particularly those traveling alone.
 Crucial Thanksgiving Travel Strategies For Non-REAL ID Travelers
 Portland airport at thanksgiving Credit: Brett Sayles / Pexels 
 Even with the $45 TSA ConfirmID options available, waiting until you reach the airport to figure out your identification situation is a gamble, especially during Thanksgiving week. A little preparation could save travelers both money and unnecessary frustration.
 The first step is checking your current driver's license. Most REAL ID-compliant licenses display a star near the top, although the exact appearance varies by state. Travelers who are uncertain should contact their state's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) rather than assuming their license qualifies.
 If you don't have an acceptable ID and plan to use the TSA ConfirmID, consider bringing additional documents that may help establish your identity. These could include credit cards, a work identification badge, or documents showing your name and address, such as a utility bill. These are not substitutes for a REAL ID or passport , and bringing them does not guarantee TSA will successfully verify your identity.
 Do TSA PreCheck And CLEAR Members Still Need a REAL ID?
 Soldier with family approaching tsa precheck at airport Credit: Shutterstock 
 Travelers enrolled in TSA PreCheck or CLEAR should not assume their membership exempts them from federal identification requirements. TSA PreCheck provides expedited security screening, while CLEAR uses biometric identity verification at participating airports. Neither program automatically replaces the requirement to present acceptable identification, and travelers without it may still be directed to additional verification.
 If you're relying on TSA ConfirmID, pay the $45 fee through Pay.gov before leaving home. This can help avoid delays caused by poor cellular service, airport Wi-Fi issues, or problems accessing the payment portal at the checkpoint.
 The TSA's $45 ConfirmID fee provides a temporary safety net for travelers who haven't upgraded to a REAL ID, but it isn't a permanent solution or a guarantee of getting through security.
 A closeup of the California Real ID driver's license focuses on the REAL ID logo. Credit: Shutterstock 
 Before heading to the airport this Thanksgiving, check your driver's license for the REAL ID star, pack a valid passport or another accepted ID if you have one, and prepay the ConfirmID fee if needed. Most importantly, allow extra time at the airport for security screening. A little preparation could help travelers avoid unexpected expenses, lengthy delays, and potentially missing their holiday flights.
 TheTravel has reached out to the TSA for additional guidance on using ConfirmID during the Thanksgiving travel rush.
